# Plastics and synthetic polymers (`polymers_plastics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by nitric_acid, sulphuric_acid, organic_structure_theory, synthetic_dyes, rubber_vulcanisation
- Core idea: Plastics are made of very long chain molecules built from small units. The first were modified natural ones: cotton treated with nitric and sulphuric acids, kneaded with camphor, gives celluloid, mouldable when warm (combs, film). Bakelite was the first fully synthetic one: phenol and formaldehyde heated together and then cured under heat and pressure set to a hard resin that never melts again, an ideal electrical insulator. Once chemists accepted that these are true giant molecules, they could design new ones on purpose: nylon, polythene, PVC, synthetic rubber.
- Pitfalls:
  - Celluloid is close kin to guncotton and burns fiercely; film stock caused cinema and archive fires.
  - The old belief that such materials are clumps of small molecules; they are single chains of thousands of units.
  - Confusing plastics that soften on heating (celluloid, polythene) with those that set for good (Bakelite).
  - Assuming plastics need oil; the early ones started from cotton, coal tar, wood spirit and milk.
- History: americas: c. 1600 BC – Mesoamerican rubber, an early deliberately processed natural polymer; 1869–1870 Hyatt's celluloid; 1907 Baekeland's Bakelite; 1935 Carothers's nylon (DuPont); europe: 1846 Schönbein's nitrocellulose; 1862 Parkes shows Parkesine; 1920 Staudinger proposes macromolecules; 1933 polythene found at ICI; 1930s PVC, polystyrene and synthetic rubber in Germany; east_asia: ancient – lacquer from the lacquer tree, a natural setting resin, at Kakinoshima in Japan about 9,000 years ago and in Neolithic China
- Read:
  - Jeffrey L. Meikle, American Plastic: A Cultural History (1995)
  - Yasu Furukawa, Inventing Polymer Science: Staudinger, Carothers, and the Emergence of Macromolecular Chemistry (1998)
